title: Edge Onboarding Lite Contract — PRD Brain Dump
content:
Purpose / quick summary:

This is a lightweight PRD brain dump for an "onramp contract" product offering: a minimal audit + approval surface that lets customers bring a customer‑managed VPC / edge network online quickly while preserving Redwood's ability to demonstrate safety/compliance at a reasonable retention/cost tradeoff.

Goal: enable 80% of small-mid enterprise private deployments to self-onboard within 2 hours using a "lite" contract that reduces evidence collection to the smallest useful set for security reviews and incident investigation.

Non‑goals:
- This is NOT a full forensic attestation system for FSI/health customers (those get the full attestation bundle).
- Not covering on‑prem air‑gapped workflows in this phase.

Context / problem we see:
- Customers want private deployments but balk at the cost/complexity of full attestation artifacts and long retention windows.
- Our current onboarding is heavy: many change snapshots, large syslog exports, and multiple approval touchpoints. That slows pilots and increases sales friction.
- Ops teams still need minimally sufficient evidence to investigate incidents and to satisfy basic compliance audits.

Primary user personas:
- Platform engineer (customer) — needs fast time to first request and lightweight evidence they can hand to internal security reviewers.
- Redwood operator (onboarding/SE) — needs clear, bounded checklist and deterministic API/contract to collect a small proof bundle and run basic gating checks.
- Customer security reviewer — needs summarized, signed statements showing who made network changes and that critical controls were on.

Key product ideas / components (high level):
1) Onramp Contract Template (signed) — a short JSON contract that both parties accept which enumerates: allowed CIDR ranges, approved service endpoints, minimum log types to collect, retention (default 30 days), and emergency rollback policy. The contract is a single machine‑parsable manifest with a human summary.

2) Minimal Evidence Bundle (MEB) — smallest set of artifacts we store/verify for the contract: 
   - change_summary.json (diff of route/NAT/security changes, user id + timestamp, short change reason)
   - connection_proof.txt (signed TLS session fingerprint and endpoint ip(s) at first successful provisioning)
   - key-rotation-marker (timestamped pointer to KMS event if used)
   - health-check-snapshot (sampled traceroute/latency/success counts, daily)
   Note: these are compressed and zipped; key point is small size and targeted fields.

3) Approval Gate Presets (lite) — three lightweight presets to map to customer risk appetite: 
   - permissive-onramp (fastest): auto-approve routine operator changes for 24h, requires human approval for new outbound endpoints.
   - standard-onramp: 1 human approver for major route/egress changes; auto for minor config.
   - conservative-onramp: 2 approvers and signed justification for anything touching firewall/egress.

4) Operator UX flows / Console surfaces (minimal):
   - "Start onramp" wizard: picks contract preset, shows estimated evidence size & retention, signs manifest (Redwood + customer admin)
   - "Change submit" quick form: select change type (route, egress, cert rotation), paste small justification, attach optional supporting link (Jira/CR), submit to gate
   - Approval inbox: compact cards with change_summary, MEB preview (one‑line), approve/deny/rollforward actions.

Minimal audit log schema (suggested fields for MEB change_summary.json):
- event_id (uuid)
- timestamp_utc
- initiator (email or service principal)
- role (customer-operator | redwood-onboarder | system)
- change_type (route | firewall | nat | cert-rotation | config)
- object_id (e.g., route table id or resource label)
- before_hash (sha256 of minimal pre-state)
- after_hash (sha256 of minimal post-state)
- justification_text (single-line, optional)
- linked_ticket (url or id, optional)
- approval_policy_used (preset name)
- approvers (list-of-emails as comma-separated string)
- signed_by (base64 signature of the manifest snippet)

Retention & cost assumptions:
- Default retention: 30 days compressed. Configurable 7–90 days.
- MEB target size per change: < 10KB (typical). If default sampling yields >100KB/day, we aggressively sample to keep costs predictable.
- Snapshot frequency defaults: daily for health, per-change for change_summary.

Rollbacks and emergency flow:
- Emergency rollback token: operator can trigger an immediate revert based on last-known stable manifest. Rollback execution requires 1 on-call Redwood operator + recorded justification. The MEB contains a rollback evidence package after execution.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Customers can complete the onramp wizard, sign the contract, and process their first successful request within 2 hours without Redwood engineering intervention.
- Approval inbox shows change cards and allows approve/deny; changes flow through selected preset.
- MEBs generated for each approved change and stored with retention policy applied.
- Search by event_id and initiator across 30-day window is < 2s median.

Open questions / risks:
- Legal: is a machine JSON manifest acceptable as a signed contract? Need Legal to validate contract language and signatures. (ask @Maya)
- Can customers supply existing SIEM forwarding in place of MEB? We need an adapter for common SIEM endpoints.
- Is 30-day default acceptable for EU customers with local regulations? Might need region-aware defaults.
- Sampling policy must be auditable — don't sample away evidence needed for a specific audit type.

Implementation notes / engineering considerations (brain dump):
- Use existing compact evidence serializer (see PD-compact-evidence repo) but add a smaller schema subset to produce MEB.
- Approval gate should be a lightweight state machine — avoid long-running orchestration complexity in MVP. Persistent state in Dynamo/PG depending on infra.
- Signatures: HMAC with cross-signed Redwood KMS key + optional customer JWK. Store signature metadata next to MEB.
- UX: keep forms minimal to avoid data quality issues; required fields only.

Next steps / TODOs:
- Sync with Legal and Security: finalize contract language (owner: Maya Lin) — target 2026-03-10.
- Prototype a tiny frontend wizard and SMS/email approval hook (owner: Ben Carter) — prototype by 2026-04-01.
- Add a "SIEM adapter" spike to accept Splunk/Datadog forwarders as alternative evidence sinks (owner: Carlos) — spike 2 weeks.
- Create acceptance test corpus (sample changes + MEBs) for SRE to run performance bench.

Notes to self / heuristics we observed in research:
- Customers repeatedly asked for a "signed short statement" they can hand to internal audit rather than tons of logs. MEB is designed to be that statement.
- UX friction mostly came from unclear justification fields. Pre-populate with templates depending on change_type.

Potential names for the product in copy: "Onramp Lite", "Compact Onramp Contract", "MEB Onramp" — prefer "Onramp Lite" for external marketing; internal code name: onramp-lite.

Meeting notes snippet (from 2025-11-05 call with ACME platform team):
- ACME asked for 14-day retention and ability to export a zip of all MEBs at project close.
- They required role-scoped approvers (no cross-team approvals).

Quick risks & mitigation summary:
- Risk: Too lightweight -> missed forensic data for real incidents. Mitigation: offer explicit upgrade path to full attest bundle; clearly surface limitations in contract.
- Risk: Customers misunderstand sampling. Mitigation: UI previews showing sample rate and example artifacts.

If this resonates, next immediate step: draft the contract JSON schema + short human-readable contract paragraph to run by Legal and Security.

END
